msItem.title: Polychronicon, etc.
msItem.note: In the second edition of Medieval Libraries of Great Britain (1964), Ker included the following footnote (p. 83, n. 4): Lambeth Palace 188, fos. 168-74, was part of Lambeth Palace 104, fos. 1-208. In MLGB3 (2010-2015), James Willoughby noted: this does not seem obvious; q.v.

supportDesc.foliation: Very large black arabic foliation numbers.

provenance.orgName: Exeter, Devon. Cathedral church of St Peter
provenance.p: Ecclesie et capitulo nostre Exon' (fol. 1r) in Grandisson's hand (erased but legible by uv light). Inscription (s. xv) on fol. 5v partly legible at line ends: ... dedit / ... Cathenandum/ ... si quis/ ... anathema habeat dei omnipotentis beate ann[e]/ ... /. Capellam appears to be legible near beginning of l. 2, and was read by M. R. James. Writing in Bishop Grandisson's hand (fol. 6r).

provenance.orgName: Ottery St Mary, Devon, Collegiate church of St Mary the Virgin
provenance.p: This attribution was rejected in the second edition of Medieval Libraries of Great Britain (1964), which did not change in the Supplement (1987). The corresponding Medieval Libraries of Great Britain index card originally recorded the following information: Three erased inscriptions. On the whole, I conjecture that it is a book left by Bishop Grandison of Exeter to his college of Ottery (M. R. James).

Ker later added the following note to the card for the rejected Ottery St Mary attribution: The two inscriptions on fol. 15 [head and foot] noted by M. R. James are now quite illegible, even by uv light, as a result of the use of reagents. That on fol. 5 is partly legible.

Ker added similar notes about the illegibility of the inscriptions to the index card for the positive Exeter attribution. There, he also wrote: Possibly the inscription on fol. 5v was of gift to the chapel of St Anne at Exeter (??). [Note that none of the published handlists included this suggestion].
